A newly laid egg of the Yellow-throated warbler (Setophaga dominica) weighs approximately 1.52 grams [Ww0 = approximately 1.52 grams], a modest initial mass that reflects the altricial developmental strategy typical of many parulids. When incubated at a constant temperature of 35 °C [T = 35 °C], embryonic development proceeds rapidly, with hatching occurring after an average of 12.5 days [ab = 12.5 days]. This incubation period, ranging from 12 to 13 days under controlled laboratory conditions, is consistent with the brief developmental times observed in other closely related wood-warblers. The relatively short embryonic phase imposes significant energetic demands on the incubating female, who must maintain stable thermal conditions within the nest cup despite fluctuations in ambient temperatures. Field observations suggest that nest attendance during this period is nearly continuous, with females departing only for brief foraging bouts. The precise thermal control of the clutch at 35 °C [T = 35 °C] appears critical for synchronizing hatching and minimizing developmental asynchrony among siblings, a factor that may influence subsequent brood survival in this single-brooded species.

Following hatching, the nestling chick experiences a period of rapid somatic growth before it is capable of independent locomotion and flight. Under the thermal conditions typical of the active breeding season, which approximate 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C] for the metabolic scope of the adult, the time since birth at fledging is approximately 10 days [tx = approximately 10 days]. This brief nestling period, during which the young bird progresses from a naked, helpless state to a fully feathered and flight-capable juvenile, is one of the shortest recorded among temperate-breeding parulids. The feather-growing nestling relies entirely on parental provisioning for its nutritional needs, and both parents contribute substantially to feeding bouts throughout the day. The rapid development trajectory is likely an evolutionary response to high nest predation pressure in this species’ preferred habitat of mature bottomland hardwood forests and cypress swamps. By minimizing the duration of the vulnerable nest-bound phase, the Yellow-throated warbler reduces the cumulative probability of nest failure due to predation by snakes, corvids, and small mammals.

Sexual maturation in the Yellow-throated warbler is attained relatively early in life, with individuals typically reaching puberty at 30 days after hatching [tp = 30 days after hatching] when assessed under standard physiological conditions of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This rapid transition from fledgling to reproductively capable adult is characteristic of small, short-lived passerines that must maximize their lifetime reproductive output within a constrained annual window. The age at first reproduction, or time since birth at first brood, thus spans approximately one full calendar year, a pattern that aligns with the migratory life history of this neotropical migrant. First-year birds that arrive late on the breeding grounds may forego nesting entirely or produce only a single clutch, whereas experienced adults are more likely to initiate nesting earlier in the season. The timing of first breeding is heavily influenced by the availability of suitable territories and the energetic condition of the individual upon arrival from its wintering grounds in the Caribbean and Central America.

These adult body masses represent the asymptotic size reached after the completion of juvenile growth and the accumulation of sufficient energy reserves for reproduction. Body condition in both sexes fluctuates seasonally, with peak mass typically recorded just prior to migration and during the early nesting phase, when fat stores are maximized to sustain the energetic demands of egg production for females and territorial defense for males. The slight difference in asymptotic mass between the sexes may reflect divergent selective pressures on foraging efficiency and flight performance during the breeding season.

The annual reproductive output of the species is limited by its single-brooded breeding system; females produce a single clutch of four eggs per year [Ri = four eggs per year], with one clutch laid annually [F_R_i = one clutch laid annually]. This constrained reproductive rate reflects a life-history strategy oriented toward high parental investment per offspring rather than maximizing fecundity, a pattern that is common among long-distance migrants that must balance the energetic costs of reproduction against the demands of a lengthy biannual migration. The relatively low maximum reproduction rate is further influenced by the brevity of the temperate breeding season and the need to complete nesting before the onset of post-breeding molt and southward departure.
